# Third-party code

## Stockfish (vendor/stockfish/)

| File | Size | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stockfish/stockfish-19-lite-single.js` | 28,230 bytes | Emscripten loader; runs as a classic Web Worker |
| `stockfish/stockfish-19-lite-single.wasm` | 1,845,971 bytes | Stockfish 19 engine with the small "lite" NNUE network |
| `stockfish/Copying.txt` | 35,821 bytes | GNU General Public License v3 |
| `stockfish/test.html` | | Manual test page for `src/sf.js` (not used by the app) |

- Source: the npm package [`stockfish`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/stockfish) **version 19.0.1**
  (Stockfish.js by Nathan Rugg, <https://github.com/nmrugg/stockfish.js>), file `bin/stockfish-19-lite-single.*`.
  The files are copied **unmodified**.
- Engine: Stockfish 19 (<https://github.com/official-stockfish/Stockfish>), "Lite, single-threaded" WASM flavour.
  It needs no `SharedArrayBuffer`, so it works on a static host such as GitHub Pages without
  COOP/COEP headers. The `.wasm` file must sit next to the `.js` file; the loader finds it by its own URL.
- License: **GPL-3.0** (see `stockfish/Copying.txt`). Knight Club is GPL-3.0 as well.
  The full Stockfish source code is available from the two repositories above.

`src/sf.js` is Knight Club's own promise wrapper around the UCI protocol (worker path
`vendor/stockfish/stockfish-19-lite-single.js`, relative to the page). To try it, serve the repository
root over HTTP (for example `python3 -m http.server`) and open `/vendor/stockfish/test.html`.
Workers cannot be loaded from `file://`; then `SF.ready()` rejects and `SF.available` is `false`.

The same engine file runs under Node.js (`node vendor/stockfish/stockfish-19-lite-single.js` speaks UCI on
stdin/stdout). `tools/gen_tactics.js` and `tools/verify_tactics.js` use it that way, so the
tactics set is checked with exactly the build that ships with the app.

## Tactics puzzles (data/tactics.json)

Generated by `tools/gen_tactics.js`, re-checked by `tools/verify_tactics.js`.

**Positions.** Games between the app's bots (levels 4-7 from `src/bots.js`, starting from the opening book)
and shallow, randomised Stockfish self-play. In roughly balanced positions the generator also tries
"plausible blunders": moves the app's 1-ply search rates within 1 pawn of its favourite but which
Stockfish says lose at least 2.5 pawns. Every candidate position comes right after a move made from a
position that was within +/-1.5 pawns, so each puzzle punishes a real mistake rather than a game that was
already decided.

**Acceptance rules** (Stockfish 19 Lite, depth 16, fresh hash for every search, MultiPV 2):
- the first move scores at least +150cp for the side to move, is at least 200cp better than the
  second-best move, and is not a forced mate (these are material puzzles; mates are in `puzzles.json`);
- the first move is not just a recapture on the square where the opponent just captured;
- the defender answers with Stockfish's best reply; every later solver move is again at least
  150cp better than the alternative;
- the line stops after the first solver move (at most 3) after which the solver is at least 2 pawns of
  material (P=1, N=B=3, R=5, Q=9) up on the puzzle start, and still at least 2 up and +150cp after the
  defender's best reply.

**Themes** are detected from the board along the solution line (heuristics in `detectThemes`):
`fork` (the moved piece attacks two targets that are the king, worth more than it, or undefended,
and one is won), `pin` (a new pin whose line wins material, attacking a pinned piece, or capturing a
pinned piece), `skewer`, `discoveredAttack`, `doubleCheck`, `hangingPiece` (a one-move capture),
`trappedPiece`, `promotion`, `backRank`, `deflection`, `sacrifice` (the solver is 2+ points down after
a defender reply that is not just recaptured), and `endgame`/`middlegame` (non-pawn material of both
sides together at most 20, or more). Some puzzles get no tactical motif beyond the phase tag.

### Tactics ratings

Each puzzle gets a difficulty estimate on the 400-2400 scale:

```
rating = 450
       + 90  * min(12, log2(nodes / 64)) // nodes the app's own engine needs before it first picks the solution
       + 60  * (findDepth - 1)         // Stockfish depth from which the solution stays its best move
       + 220 * (n - 1)                 // n = number of solver moves (1-3)
       + 15  * max(0, tempting - 3)    // tempting = legal checks + captures in the start position
       + 150 if the first move is quiet (no check, no capture)
       + 150 if the line contains a sacrifice
       - 150 if the puzzle is a single capture of an undefended piece
clamped to 400..2400, rounded to 10
```

Reasoning: the app's alpha-beta engine at a small node budget behaves much like a club player who
calculates a little; the more nodes it needs (doubling steps from 64; capped at 262,144, beyond which its choice says more about its own blind spots than about the position), the less obvious the move.
Stockfish's discovery depth adds a second view for deep ideas. Longer lines need more calculation, many
checks and captures give more ways to go wrong, and quiet moves and sacrifices are the classic reasons
people miss tactics. The ratings are estimates on the same scale as the checkmate puzzles, not
measured from human solving data.
